newsitem.title: USA: U.S. feedlot cattle unaffected by heat wave.
newsitem.headline: U.S. feedlot cattle unaffected by heat wave.

text.p: Cattle in feedlots from Nebraska to Texas have yet to show significant effects from this week's heat wave and that should continue as long as the humidity remains low and the breezes continue, cattlemen said.
"It hasn't really been a factor for us yet," said Kris Kahn, referring to this week's heat.

Kahn, a market analyst with the Texas Cattle Feeders Association (TCFA), said cattle weight gains have largely been unaffected by the 90-degree Fahrenheit weather because the humidity has remained low.
The breezes that have accompanied the heat have helped.

"If we got up into the high 90s without any breeze it would probably hurt consumption and then next you would see cattle weighing up lighter," said Lyle Koons, a manager at Caprock Feeders, Amarillo, Texas.

TCFA's Kahn said cattle have been marketed at lighter weights recently but that has been due to active cattle marketings. Last week cattle sold for slaughter throughout the U.S. averaged 1,162 lbs versus 1,165 the previous year.
Kansas cattle have survived the heat, thanks to timely breezes and low humdity, feedlot sources there said.

"It can be 100 degrees here and most of the time we don't have the humidity that can hurt cattle," said a Kansas feedlot manager. "Plus if the wind blows a little, which is what usually happens, it will help them. If it gets dead still the cattle are going to suffer and they will back off the feed."

Weather Services Corp said the 90-degree weather should continue at least until early next week from Nebraska to the Texas Panhandle, with readings in the high 90s likely at the southern boundary of that area.

The hot, dry weather created pockets of dry pastures in Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, but overall pastures in those states were rated mostly good to excellent as of Sunday by the states' agricultural statistics services.
"The heat hasn't been much of a story at all," said Jeff Stolle, vice president of marketing for Nebraska Cattlemen's Association.
As in Texas, Nebraska's heat has been accompanied by breezes and low humidity which has minimized the stress on cattle, Stolle said.
